questions.problem:
Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{1}{8}(4-x)({x}^{2}+6)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
The equation is already fully factored. Note that the discriminant of ${x}^{2}+6=0$ is 

$$
D={0}^{2}-4(1)(6)=-24<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the function $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=4.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by plugging the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{8}(4-0)({0}^{2}+6) \\  & =\frac{(4)(6)}{8} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at the point $(0,3),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=4,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph has an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/review-13925710/assets/q-28197-e-0.png)

provenance.knowledge_point_title: Graphing a Factored Cubic Curve with a Negative Leading Coefficient

questions.problem:
Given that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x)={x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+5x-6,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-2)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 2 & 1 & -3 & 5 & -6 \\  &  & 2 & -2 & 6 \\  & 1 & -1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x-2}={x}^{2}-x+3
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x-2)({x}^{2}-x+3).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of ${x}^{2}-x+3=0$ is 

$$
D=(1{)}^{2}-4(1)(3)=-11<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=2.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={0}^{3}-3(0{)}^{2}+5(0)-6=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-6),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=2,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/review-13925710/assets/q-39032-a-1.png)

questions.problem:
Given that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+4,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-2)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\  &  & -2 & -2 & -4 \\  & -1 & -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x-2} & =-{x}^{2}-x-2 \\  & =-({x}^{2}+x+2),\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=-(x-2)({x}^{2}+x+2).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $({x}^{2}+x+2)=0$ is 

$$
D={1}^{2}-4(1)(2)=-7<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=2.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
y=-(0{)}^{3}+(0{)}^{2}+4=4
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,4),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=2,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph has an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/review-13925710/assets/q-39091-a-1.png)

questions.problem:
Given that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x)=7{x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+x-1,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-1)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 1 & 7 & -7 & 1 & -1 \\  &  & 7 & 0 & 1 \\  & 7 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x-1}=7{x}^{2}+1
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x-1)(7{x}^{2}+1).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $7{x}^{2}+1=0$ is 

$$
D=(0{)}^{2}-4(7)(1)=-28<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=1.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7(0{)}^{3}-7(0{)}^{2}+0-1=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-1),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=1,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/review-13925710/assets/q-112434-a-1.png)
